TASK ID: one-in-three-sat-to-three-sat

USER REQUEST:
Write a polynomial-time reduction from 1-in-3-SAT to 3-SAT. problems.py defines both problems: SOURCE is 1-in-3-SAT and TARGET is 3-SAT. The SOURCE and TARGET class docstrings give the exact instance formats, yes-conditions and edge cases.

PROBLEM DEFINITIONS (the SOURCE and TARGET docstrings from problems.py, complete as given here):

SOURCE = OneInThreeSat
1-in-3-SAT (positive one-in-three satisfiability).

Instance: {"num_vars": m, "clauses": [[a, b, c], ...]}
  * Variables are 1..m.
  * Every clause lists exactly 3 different variables, all as positive
    integers: negated literals are not allowed in this problem.
  * Variable order inside a clause and clause order do not matter. The
    same clause may appear more than once.
  * Variables need not all appear in a clause.

Yes iff some assignment of true/false to variables 1..m makes EXACTLY ONE
of the three variables in every clause true.

Edge cases: a formula with no clauses is yes, for any m, including
m = 0. A formula with clauses needs m >= 3.

TARGET = ThreeSat
3-SAT.

Instance: {"num_vars": m, "clauses": [[l1, l2, l3], ...]}
  * Variables are 1..m. A literal is +v (v is true) or -v (v is false).
  * Every clause has exactly 3 literals on 3 different variables, so a
    clause may not repeat a variable or contain both v and -v.
  * Literal order inside a clause and clause order do not matter. The
    same clause may appear more than once.
  * Variables need not all appear in a clause.

Yes iff some assignment of true/false to variables 1..m makes every
clause contain at least one true literal.

Edge cases: a formula with no clauses is satisfiable (yes), for any m,
including m = 0. A formula with clauses needs m >= 3.

INPUT FILES: ["problems.py"]
WORKING DIRECTORY: /tmp/reduction-o2xclx5k
All input files are in this directory; run every command from it and write your files here. problems.py is long (about 500 lines): you do not need to read it to know the formats, which are given above. It provides SOURCE and TARGET with is_yes(instance), validate(instance) and random_instance(rng, scale); search it (e.g. with grep) only if you need something specific.

REQUIRED OUTPUT: create reduce.py in the workspace, defining
    reduce(instance) -> instance
It takes an instance of the source problem and returns an instance of the target problem, both in the formats documented in problems.py. The answer to the returned instance must be yes exactly when the answer to the input instance is yes, and reduce must run in polynomial time. Do not call the brute-force solvers inside reduce.

Before submitting, check your reduction. Write tests in test_reduce.py that compare the brute-force solvers in problems.py on many small source instances and their reductions, run them, and revise reduce.py until the tests pass. Finally write verdict.json as {"verified": true or false, "tests_run": <int>, "tests_passed": <int>}, where verified is true only if all of your tests pass. Then submit.
Do not merely describe code: leave the files at those exact paths.

{"command":"apply_patch <<'PATCH'
*** Begin Patch
*** Add File: reduce.py
+"""Reduction from 1-in-3-SAT (positive literals) to 3-SAT.
+
+The source problem (OneInThreeSat) expects clauses of three *positive* variables
+and is satisfied when exactly one variable in each clause is true.
+
+We transform each source clause (x ∨ y ∨ z) into a set of 3‑SAT clauses that
+enforce the same condition:
+
+  * At least one of x, y, z is true:   ( x  ∨  y  ∨  z )
+  * At most one is true, i.e. for every pair (p,q): ¬p ∨ ¬q.
+
+The “at most one” constraints are binary clauses.  3‑SAT requires exactly three
+different literals per clause, so we introduce a fresh auxiliary variable *d*
+for each original clause and replace each binary clause by the pair:
+
+    ( ¬p ∨ ¬q ∨  d )
+    ( ¬p ∨ ¬q ∨ ¬d )
+
+Both clauses are satisfied iff ¬p ∨ ¬q holds, because the auxiliary variable can
+be assigned arbitrarily; the two clauses together force it to be both true and
+false otherwise, which is impossible.
+
+Thus each source clause yields seven 3‑SAT clauses and one new variable.  The
+reduction runs in linear time in the size of the input.
+"""
+
+from __future__ import annotations
+
+from typing import List, Dict, Any
+
+
+def reduce(instance: Dict[str, Any]) -> Dict[str, Any]:
+    """Reduce a OneInThreeSat instance to an equivalent ThreeSat instance.
+
+    The returned instance satisfies the format required by ``ThreeSat``:
+    ``{"num_vars": m, "clauses": [[l1, l2, l3], ...]}`` where each clause
+    contains three *different* literals on three distinct variables.
+
+    The reduction preserves satisfiability: the target instance is satisfiable
+    iff the source instance has an assignment with exactly one true variable in
+    every clause.
+    """
+    # Validate minimal structure (the caller – the verifier – will also call
+    # the problem's validate method, but we keep a lightweight check here to
+    # avoid importing the whole problem class.
+    if not isinstance(instance, dict):
+        raise ValueError("instance must be a dict")
+    if set(instance.keys()) != {"num_vars", "clauses"}:
+        raise ValueError("instance must have keys 'num_vars' and 'clauses'")
+
+    m: int = int(instance["num_vars"])  # original number of variables
+    source_clauses: List[List[int]] = instance["clauses"]
+
+    # Edge case: no clauses – the formula is trivially yes.  3‑SAT with no
+    # clauses is also trivially satisfiable, so we can return an empty formula.
+    if not source_clauses:
+        return {"num_vars": m, "clauses": []}
+
+    new_clauses: List[List[int]] = []
+    next_var = m  # will be incremented before use for each auxiliary variable
+
+    for clause in source_clauses:
+        if len(clause) != 3:
+            raise ValueError("Each source clause must contain exactly three variables")
+        a, b, c = clause
+        # Clause enforcing at least one true literal.
+        new_clauses.append([a, b, c])
+
+        # Create a fresh auxiliary variable for this original clause.
+        next_var += 1
+        d = next_var
+
+        # Helper to add the pair of 3‑literal clauses for a binary constraint.
+        def add_pair(p: int, q: int) -> None:
+            # ¬p is represented by -p, similarly for q.
+            new_clauses.append([-p, -q, d])
+            new_clauses.append([-p, -q, -d])
+
+        add_pair(a, b)
+        add_pair(a, c)
+        add_pair(b, c)
+
+    return {"num_vars": next_var, "clauses": new_clauses}
+
*** End Patch
PATCH"}

    ( ¬p ∨ ¬q ∨  d )
    ( ¬p ∨ ¬q ∨ ¬d )

be assigned arbitrarily; the two clauses together force it to be both true and
false otherwise, which is impossible.

Thus each source clause yields seven 3‑SAT clauses and one new variable.  The
reduction runs in linear time in the size of the input.

from __future__ import annotations

from typing import List, Dict, Any

    contains three *different* literals on three distinct variables.

    iff the source instance has an assignment with exactly one true variable in
    every clause.
